name: Ben Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior cook at The Plough, a steak and carvery place on the edge of town by the ring road. Weekdays I'm on the steak grill, sides and sauces, and Sundays it's the carvery, carving three hundred plates of beef and turkey. Stuart, the head chef, is teaching me to cook steak by touch instead of the probe, and I'm getting there. It's hot and loud, but I like a hard day's work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Grace, she's a teaching assistant at the primary school. Wedding's next August, at our church, and we're paying for most of it ourselves. I've got less than a month's money in the bank, because it all goes on the wedding pot and rent. I use AI now and then, Grace showed me how to make a wedding budget with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I always thought it was overhyped. At work we'd joke about the robot carvery that never came. At church I'd say hard work still counts, which I believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's okay for me. The Plough is always busy, Sunday lunch especially, and my job's safe as long as I keep improving. The pressure is the wedding and the rent, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my shifts, ask Stuart for extra Saturdays, and put every bit of overtime into the wedding pot. I'd ask about the chef apprenticeship the brewery that owns The Plough runs, so I can move up to a proper section. And I'd keep using the AI for the wedding budget, it's handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. A bit stretched by the wedding, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wedding cost look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About nine thousand all in, which is a lot on our wages. Grace's parents are giving two, the church hall is cheap, and my aunties are cooking. We've got about four thousand so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if something goes wrong before then, like losing shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the wedding gets smaller, not later. We'd still marry, maybe just a buffet in the hall. My fiancée Grace says she'd marry me in the car park if she had to.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped**, as I always thought.
I'd say at church that **hard work** still counts.
think: The Plough stays busy, so my **job's safe** if I keep improving.
The real pressure is the **wedding and rent**.
do: Ask the head chef for **extra Saturdays** and bank the overtime.
Apply for the brewery's **chef apprenticeship** to move up a section.
Keep using AI for the **wedding budget**.
S0.quote: My fiancée Grace says she'd marry me in the car park if she had to.
fieldNote: Ben's pressure is a **self-funded wedding**, not technology.
He sees the **brewery apprenticeship** as the proper way up.
He uses AI **practically**, for a budget his fiancée set up.

steps.text: Work extra Saturday shifts on the steak grill at The Plough
Put all overtime pay into the wedding pot
Apply for the brewery's chef apprenticeship scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and you either learn or you get left behind. At work I'd say the cooking's safe, it's the bookings and the till that change. At church I'd tell the young lads to get an apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the brewery cuts office jobs and maybe the kitchen gets ordering software. That's fine by me. The carvery still needs someone to carve, and I'm hands-on all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the apprenticeship, two years, one day a week at college. I'd learn whatever ordering system the brewery brings in, once Stuart's shown me. We'd keep the wedding on track, nothing changes there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for other people, fine for me, I think. Grace worries about the school, but that's people work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Grace worry about at the school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That AI marking and reading apps mean fewer teaching assistants. But no app calms a crying six-year-old the way my fiancée Grace does at the school. I tell her that, and she says I'm biased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at The Plough would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mandy on the bookings phone, she's been there twenty years. If the brewery puts in an online booking bot, she's gone. She knows every regular by name.

say: I'd say you **learn** or get left behind.
I'd tell the young lads at church to get an **apprenticeship**.
think: The brewery cuts **office jobs**, and the kitchen just gets ordering software.
The carvery still needs **someone to carve**, so I'm fine.
do: Do the **two-year apprenticeship**, one day a week at college.
Learn the brewery's **ordering system** once the head chef shows me.
feel: **Fine for me**, uneasy for others like his fiancée.
S1.quote: No app calms a crying six-year-old the way my fiancée Grace does at the school.
fieldNote: Ben sees **office roles** at the brewery as the ones at risk.
His instinct is **apprenticeship**, which fits his traditional views.
He worries for **a long-serving colleague** on the booking phone.

steps.text: Start the two-year chef apprenticeship with weekly college days
Learn the brewery's new kitchen ordering system from Stuart
Keep saving to hold the August wedding date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this was rushed, and the people pushing it didn't think about ordinary families. At work I'd say keep your head and keep earning. At church I'd say pray, then plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be worried. The brewery would cut anything a computer can do straight away, and robots could carve and grill by 2031. I'd be married three years, maybe with a baby, and out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still marry in August, but small, just the church and a buffet, and put the rest into savings. I'd look for an electrician apprenticeship in the first year, because robots will need wiring and old houses need fixing. I'd use AI to help with the maths, which I was bad at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's shifting under the wedding plans. Scared, but I'd try not to show Grace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Chidi is one, and he says he's turning work away. It's hands-on, it's a proper trade, and you can work for yourself. Robots for wiring in old houses feel a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Grace decide about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait. We both want three children, but not with no job. That's the bit that would hurt most.

say: I'd say AGI was **rushed** without thought for ordinary families.
I'd tell church to **pray, then plan**.
At work I'd tell people to **keep earning** and keep their heads.
think: I could be married three years and **out of work**.
The brewery would cut anything a **computer can do** straight away.
do: Hold a **small wedding** in August and save the rest.
Find an **electrician apprenticeship** in the first year.
Use AI to help with the **maths** I was bad at.
feel: **Scared**, hiding it from his fiancée as the wedding plans shift.
S2.quote: We both want three children, but not with no job.
fieldNote: Ben expects to **lose his cook job** by about 2031.
He turns to a **family trade** through his uncle, an electrician.
He'd shrink the wedding and **delay children**.

steps.text: Shrink the August wedding to church and a hall buffet
Start an electrician apprenticeship with his uncle Chidi
Use AI tools to practise the maths for the electrical course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, so use it. At work I'd say learn a second skill. At church I'd tell people to look after their families first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have about eight years before robots do my job. That's enough to finish the chef apprenticeship and then start something else. I'd be anxious, but I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry next August as planned, full wedding. In year two I'd talk to my uncle about the electrician route, maybe doing his labouring on Mondays. We'd save for a house deposit later, not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can live with it. It's like a long journey with a known end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said children wait in the fast one. What about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one, in a couple of years. Grace would want to. We'd decide once I'm in the trade properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd say to Stuart, the head chef?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thank you, mostly. He took a chance on me. The best thing the head chef taught me was to learn something properly, even if I end up using it somewhere else.

say: I'd say five years is **fair warning**.
I'd tell workmates to **learn a second skill**.
I'd tell church to look after **families first**.
think: I'd have about **eight years** before robots do my job.
There's time to **finish the apprenticeship** and then switch.
do: Labour for my uncle on **Mondays** from year two.
feel: **Worried**, like a long journey with a known end.
S3.quote: The best thing the head chef taught me was to learn something properly, even if I end up using it somewhere else.
fieldNote: Ben stays **anxious** because he still expects the cook job to end.
He stages his plan: **chef apprenticeship first**, trade second.
He shows real **gratitude** to his head chef.

steps.text: Hold the full church wedding next August as planned
Labour for his uncle's electrical business on Mondays
Open a savings account for a future house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so no excuses. At work I'd say this is a career, so plan it. At church I'd say the same thing my dad says, God gives you time, don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be fine, I think. Thirteen years until robots cook, I'd be forty, settled, with kids. I'd be well into a trade by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the chef apprenticeship, enjoy cooking for a few years, and watch which way it goes. Around year five I'd start the electrician course at college. We'd have our first child about then too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. Uneasy in the background, but more like the weather than a storm warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade with your hands and your head. Don't wait for someone to give you a job. That's what my dad told me, and I'd pass it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this one that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some people would waste the ten years and think robot cooks are far away. My mates at the pub laugh it off. I worry about them more than me.

say: I'd say ten years means **no excuses**.
I'd share my dad's line: **God gives you time**, don't waste it.
think: I'd be **forty and settled** when robots cook.
I'd be **well into a trade** by then.
The real risk is people treating ten years as **far away**.
do: Finish the **chef apprenticeship** and cook for a few years.
Start the **electrician course** around year five.
S4.quote: Some people would waste the ten years and think robot cooks are far away.
fieldNote: With time, Ben **waits and watches** before switching trades.
Family milestones, the **wedding and a child**, frame his plan.
He worries more about **friends** who laugh it off.

steps.text: Watch for five years how kitchen robots spread
Start the college electrician course around year five
Plan the first child for around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would land right on top of the wedding and our first years married, with nothing saved. What would help is paid apprenticeships, real ones, where you earn while you learn. Not handouts, a ladder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about church and community. When things go wrong around here, it's the church that cooks the meals and finds people work. That's what holds a town together.

headlineQuote: When things go wrong around here, it's the church that cooks the meals and finds people work.
portrait: Ben is a 27-year-old **junior cook** at a busy steak and carvery restaurant.
He's engaged to Grace, a **teaching assistant**, and saving for a self-funded wedding.
He's traditional, believes in **apprenticeships** over handouts, and uses AI now and then.
Fast AGI **alarms** him because it lands on the wedding and early married years.
His escape route is an **electrician trade** through his uncle.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, landing on the wedding with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships** where you earn while you learn.
